blocks.text: Quick verdict

Oxylabs is the strongest enterprise replacement for NetNut: its 175M+ residential pool, published 99.95% success rate, dedicated ISP and datacenter proxies and Web Scraper API cover everything NetNut sold, and its formal ethical-sourcing documentation answers the question NetNut's collapse raised. It costs more at entry ($8/GB pay-as-you-go), but its Corporate plan reaches $2.50/GB, in the same range NetNut charged at volume. For enterprise scraping and ad-verification teams, it is the lowest-risk move.

Oxylabs vs NetNut was once a comparison between two enterprise-oriented networks known for ISP proxies and fast residential traffic. Since the FBI seized NetNut's domains on July 2, 2026, after Google linked its exit nodes to the Popa botnet, enterprise teams have needed a replacement that procurement can sign off on. This page explains NetNut's status, compares Oxylabs with what NetNut offered, and lays out a migration plan.
What happened to NetNut?

On July 2, 2026, the FBI, working with IRS Criminal Investigation, Google, Lumen and the Shadowserver Foundation, seized hundreds of domains tied to NetNut, the residential proxy service owned by Nasdaq-listed Alarum Technologies. Google's Threat Intelligence Group said NetNut's exit-node pool overlapped with Popa, a botnet it estimated at about two million consumer devices, many of them smart TVs and streaming boxes. Alarum disputes the botnet label and said it would cooperate with law enforcement, but netnut.com and, within days, netnut.io displayed federal seizure notices. As of October 2026 the service is not something you can responsibly buy or rely on.

blocks.text: Oxylabs in 2026: what you get

Oxylabs is a Lithuanian web-data company and Bright Data's closest rival at the top of the market. It advertises a residential pool of more than 175 million IPs across 195 locations, publishes a 99.95% success rate for residential traffic, and sells seven product lines including datacenter, ISP and mobile proxies, a Web Scraper API and Web Unblocker. Onboarding is more sales-led than the mid-market providers, but self-service has expanded through 2026, including dedicated ISP proxies.

Oxylabs sells enterprise-grade proxy infrastructure with a strong reputation among large scraping teams. Its residential network is one of the two largest on the market (175M+ advertised IPs, 195 locations), targeting reaches city, ZIP and ASN level, and its scraper APIs bundle rendering and parsing so you buy results rather than gigabytes. The weak spot for smaller buyers is entry cost: pay-as-you-go runs $8/GB and the cheapest monthly rate needs a $2,500 commitment.

Strengths: One of the two largest residential pools available; Published 99.95% residential success rate; Strong scraper APIs that bill per result; Formal ethical-sourcing documentation for procurement. Weak spots: Expensive at low volume ($8/GB PAYG); Best rates need large monthly commitments; Residential trial goes through sales rather than self-service.
What NetNut offered, and how Oxylabs compares

Before the seizure, NetNut was best known for ISP-sourced static residential proxies and a fast rotating residential network aimed at scraping, ad verification and brand-protection teams. Its residential rates generally ran from about $1.87 to $3.53 per GB on larger plans, with higher effective prices on entry plans. Oxylabs covers much of the same ground: datacenter, dedicated datacenter, isp, mobile, web scraper api, web unblocker, headless browser sit alongside its residential network, which advertises 175M+ IPs in 195 countries.
What former NetNut customers need, and whether Oxylabs
delivers

Most NetNut accounts were built around three things: static ISP IPs for long-lived sessions, rotating residential traffic with US state and city targeting, and high concurrency for scraping. On static ISP-style IPs, Oxylabs's answer is yes; its other products are datacenter, dedicated datacenter, ISP, mobile, Web Scraper API, Web Unblocker, headless browser. On rotating residential targeting, Oxylabs offers country, state, city, ZIP and ASN in 195 countries, with rotating and sticky sessions on residential and mobile. On billing, Oxylabs uses pay-as-you-go or monthly plans, and unused traffic is handled as follows: monthly plan allowances reset each cycle. Map each of your old NetNut zones to one of these before you migrate, so nothing breaks on the day you switch.
Oxylabs pricing

Oxylabs charges $8/GB pay-as-you-go for residential traffic. Monthly plans start with Starter at $30 for 5 GB ($6/GB) and a Basic tier around $100 for 20 GB, and the rate falls to $2.50/GB on the $2,500/month Corporate plan. Mobile traffic starts at $7.50/GB.

Quick cost check for Oxylabs: 10 GB comes to $80 PAYG, or $100 Basic plan for 20 GB, and 100 GB comes to mid-tier plans priced inside the dashboard. NetNut's larger plans used to run about $1.87-$3.53/GB, so compare against what you actually paid rather than NetNut's headline rate.
How to migrate from NetNut to Oxylabs
1. Export your NetNut usage history and list the countries, cities and session types you actually used, so you can map them to Oxylabs's targeting (country, state, city, ZIP and ASN).

2. Test before you commit. Oxylabs's testing option: residential trial arranged through sales, once per customer. Run your real targets for a day on the smallest purchase before moving production traffic.
3. Swap the gateway host and credentials in your scraper or browser profiles. Oxylabs supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5.
4. Compare success rate, response time and cost per successful request against your old NetNut baseline, then move traffic over in stages.
5. Remove any NetNut SDKs, browser extensions or endpoints from your systems, and rotate any credentials that were stored alongside them.
Where Oxylabs fits best
General web scraping: strong fit. Why: its pool size and Web Scraper API suit large crawls.
SERP and rank tracking: strong fit. Why: its scraper API returns parsed search results.
Social media and multi-account management: workable. Why: it works, but the pricing is built for volume, not a handful of accounts.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: strong fit. Why: city and ZIP targeting plus parsed e-commerce endpoints.
Ad verification and geo-testing: strong fit. Why: broad geo coverage with ASN targeting.
Tight budgets: weak fit. Why: entry pricing is among the highest in this comparison.
Protocols and sessions

Oxylabs supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5 and offers rotating and sticky sessions on residential and mobile. Targeting covers country, state, city, ZIP and ASN across 195 countries. Like NetNut's residential gateway, it works through a single backconnect endpoint with location and session options passed in the username, plus IP whitelisting.
How to vet a residential proxy provider after NetNut

NetNut's customers did not choose to route traffic through a botnet; they bought what looked like a standard enterprise service. The lesson is to check sourcing before you buy, not after. Whichever provider replaces NetNut for you, Oxylabs included, run through these checks:
How are residential IPs sourced? Look for an opt-in SDK or app programme with clear user
consent and compensation, and ask which partner apps are involved.
Does the provider publish an ethics or sourcing policy, and has it been audited or certified (for
example AppEsteem or ISO 27001)?
What KYC does the provider apply to customers, and which target categories are restricted?
Strict onboarding is a good sign, not an inconvenience.
How does it handle abuse reports, and is there a named legal entity and jurisdiction behind the
service?
Can you get contractual assurances, such as a data-processing agreement, if your compliance
team needs them?
Bottom line

NetNut is no longer a provider you can plan around, so the real decision is which network replaces it. Oxylabs is strongest for large scraping pipelines with steady volume and teams that want a managed scraper API option, starts at $8/GB pay-as-you-go; Starter plan $30 for 5 GB ($6/GB), and offers residential trial arranged through sales, once per customer. Test it on your own targets for a day, compare cost per successful request with your old NetNut baseline, and move production traffic in stages.
